title: Winter break activities for kids: a screen-light, learning-friendly plan
summary: A flexible winter break plan with screen-light activities for kids, from kitchen projects to cozy reading, plus easy ways to keep learning without a worksheet.
body_markdown:
## Reading, writing, and quiet time


A cozy reading routine is easier to start in winter than at almost any other time of year. Try a read-aloud after dinner, even with kids who read on their own, since it gives everyone a shared story to look forward to. Let kids choose the book, and let a graphic novel count.


For writing, a small notebook goes a long way. Kids can keep a break journal with one sentence a day, write a comic about the week, or answer a question from[60 questions to get your kids to open up](https://outschool.com/articles/60-questions-ask-kids) at dinner. If your child likes made-up stories,[50 creative writing prompts for kids](https://outschool.com/articles/creative-writing-prompts-kids) has plenty to start from. Teens often prefer something low-pressure, like a short letter to a relative or a journal built around a playlist.


## Getting outside, even when it's cold


Bundled-up kids can handle more cold than many parents expect, and a short outing often resets a restless afternoon. Try a neighborhood scavenger hunt for animal tracks and bare-branch shapes, a winter weather log where kids record the temperature and sky each day, or an after-dark walk to look at lights. Older kids can graph the temperatures by the end of the break.


If it's too icy to go out, a living-room obstacle course and a dance party count as movement.


## Learning that doesn't feel like school


Some families like a little structure over break, mostly so the first week back in January isn't a shock. These are a few low-key ways to keep skills warm:


- **Math:** Let kids plan and budget a family movie night or a small outing, including snacks, and add up the total.
- **Reading:** Keep a basket of library books in the living room, and let kids trade recommendations at dinner.
- **Writing:** Have kids write thank-you notes for gifts, which gives them a real reader and a real reason to write.
- **History:** Ask a grandparent or relative about a winter tradition they remember, and have your child write down or record the answers.
- **Science:** Track sunrise and sunset times around the winter solstice, which falls around December 21, and talk about why the days change.


For a gentle end-of-break reset, you can also set a few goals together.[New year planning](https://outschool.com/articles/new-year-homeschooling-goals) shows how one Outschool teacher approaches it.


## When the plan falls apart


Some days nothing sticks, and that's normal. Keep a short backup list somewhere visible for those afternoons.[Boredom busters: 36 easy activities for kids](https://outschool.com/articles/easy-activities-kids) and[Twenty enriching indoor activities for kids](https://outschool.com/articles/twenty-enriching-indoor-activities-for-kids) are both good places to borrow from.


## When a live class helps


After a week at home, some kids want other kids, or a teacher who isn't mom or dad. A live class can give a restless week some shape, and many families treat it differently from scrolling because kids are talking, making, and learning with a teacher and other kids. You can browse[enrichment classes](https://outschool.com/online-classes/enrichment) to see what's available, or look at[cooking classes](https://outschool.com/online-classes/cooking) ,[art classes](https://outschool.com/online-classes/art) , and[creative writing classes](https://outschool.com/online-classes/creative-writing) . Screen-light doesn't have to mean screen-free.


## Watch for


Watch for plans so full that the break stops feeling like a break. Two or three anchors a week is plenty. It's also worth watching the afternoon slump, when screens often creep back in, and having a snack and a project already set out can help. If the plan starts to stress you out, shrink it.


## FAQ


### How much screen time is okay over winter break?


There isn't one number that works for every family. The American Academy of Pediatrics focuses on the quality of media use and on making room for sleep, movement, and time together, rather than on a set limit. \[1\] Many families choose a few screen-free times, like meals and the hour before bed, and let the rest flex.


### Do kids need to keep up with school over winter break?


It depends on your family. Some skip schoolwork entirely, while others like a little reading and a project or two to keep skills warm.


### What are good winter break activities for teens?


Teens often respond to projects with a real outcome and some choice, like cooking dinner for the family once a week, building something, learning an instrument, or writing a short story to share. Giving them a say in the plan usually goes over better than handing them an assignment.


### What if we're traveling or having lots of visitors?


Pack a small activity bag with a notebook, a deck of cards, and a book, and keep one anchor, like an evening read-aloud, going wherever you are.
